In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat al-Fajr

It is Meccan.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿By the dawn﴾. Abu Salih narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is the dawn of Muharram, which is the first day of it. In another narration from him, it is the dawn of the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr). It is also said: it is the dawn of every day.

And His saying: ﴿By the ten nights﴾. Most of the opinions are that they are the ten (nights) of Dhu al-Hijjah. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, in one narration, that they are the last ten (nights) of Ramadan. It is reported from Masruq that they are the ten about which Allah the Exalted said in the story of Musa: ﴿And We completed it with ten﴾. And it is reported from some of them that they are the first ten (nights) of Muharram.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 89, verse 3:

And His saying: ﴿By the even and the odd﴾. ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that it (the even and the odd) refers to the prayer: among it there is an even (shaf') and among it there is an odd (witr). Abū ʿĪsā (al-Tirmidhī) narrated it in his Jāmiʿ.

The second opinion: the even is the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-naḥr), and the odd is the Day of ʿArafah. Some narrated this traced back (marfūʿ) to the Prophet (ﷺ).

It is also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās.

This is a well-known opinion.

And from Ibn al-Zubayr: the even is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But whoever hastens in two days﴾. So the first two days of the days of stoning (al-ramy) are the even, and the third day is the odd.

Hushaym narrated from Mughīrah, from Ibrāhīm, that the even is the pair (zawj) and the odd is the single (fard).

Mujāhid said: it is the whole number, of which there is the even and of which there is the odd, and this is close to the saying of Ibrāhīm.

And from ʿAṭāʾ, who said: the even is the first ten days of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, and the odd is the days of tashrīq.

And from a group of them who said: the even is the creation (al-khalq), and the odd is God, Exalted is He.

It is also said: the even is Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ, and the odd is God.

The reading "wa-l-witr" with a fatḥah (wa-l-watr) is also recited, and the philologists said: the fatḥah and the kasrah (witr/watr) have the same meaning.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 89, verse 4:

And His saying: ﴿And the night when it passes by﴾. Abu al-'Aliyah said: "When it approaches." Ibrahim (al-Nakha'i) said: "When it becomes level (or stands still)." And it is related from some of them that "idha yasr" means: when it is traveled through (yusra fihi), so that some of it follows upon the other. It was also said: it is traveled through (yusra fihi).

It has been interpreted as the night of Jam', and it is the night of the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr).

And His saying: ﴿Is there not in that an oath for one of understanding?﴾ That is: for one who has intellect ('aql).

Al-Farra' said: "For one of understanding" means: for one who controls himself and restrains his desire.

It is also said: "For one of understanding" means: for one who possesses judgment (hukm). Al-hajr (ḥajr) in the language means prevention, and al-hijr (ḥijr) is derived from it. Intellect was called ḥijr because it prevents a person from ugly deeds. And this is for emphasis of the oath, and it is not the thing sworn to.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 89, verse 6–7:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd, Iram?﴾ [Iram] is the name of the forefather of ʿĀd, for they said: he is ʿĀd the son of Iram, son of ʿAwṣ, son of Sām, son of Nūḥ (Noah). Among them are those who said: it is the name of a city. For this reason it is not declined (ghayr munṣarif). If we say it is the name of a man, we do not decline it because it is a non-Arabic name (ism aʿjamī).

It is related from Mālik ibn Anas that Iram is the district (kūrah) of Damascus.

It is related from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī that it is Alexandria.

His saying: ﴿dhāt al-ʿimād﴾ means: possessing lofty buildings. This is if we say that Iram is the name of a city.

The second opinion: His saying ﴿dhāt al-ʿimād﴾ means: possessing tall bodies. It is said: "a man is muʿammad" when he is tall. According to this, ʿĀd is the name of the tribe, and His saying ﴿dhāt al-ʿimād﴾ refers to the tribe.

In the narrative (al-qiṣṣah): the height of the tallest of them was five hundred cubits (dhirāʿ), and the shortest was three hundred.

It is related from Abū Hurayrah that he said: One of them would lift a leaf of a door made of stone, and five hundred men of yours could not carry it. Mujāhid said: dhāt ʿimād means dhāt ʿamūd (possessing pillars), and the meaning is that they were people of tents who did not settle in one place, but moved in search of pasture (yantajiʿūn li-ṭalab al-kalaʾ), that is, they moved from place to place. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: dhāt al-ʿimād means dhāt al-quwwah (possessing strength), derived from the strength of pillars.

In the narrative: ʿAwj ibn ʿUnuq was among them.

al-Naqqāsh mentioned: the height of Mūsā was seven cubits, his staff was seven cubits, and his leap was seven cubits, so he struck Kaʿb ʿAwj ibn ʿUnuq and killed him.

Also among what is transmitted in the stories: one of his ribs was a bridge for the people of Egypt for so-and-so many years, that is, it was a bridge for them over the Nile. In the exegesis it is said that ʿĀd are two: the first ʿĀd and the other ʿĀd. The first ʿĀd is ʿĀd of Iram, and the second ʿĀd is the well-known ʿĀd, and it is they to whom the Prophet Hūd (peace be upon him) was sent.

Ibn Qays al-Ruqayyāt said:
(A glory ancient, its first foundation built by one who reached ʿĀd and before him Iram.)

And His saying: ﴿which had not been created the like of in the lands﴾ means: the like of their bodies had not been created in the lands.

And in the narration of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Mas'ud: "who had not been created the like of them in the lands."

and as for His saying: ﴿And Thamud, who hewed the rock in the valley﴾ — they cut through and hollowed out; and it is in the sense of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they used to hew out houses from the mountains, secure﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 89, verse 10:

And His saying: ﴿And Pharaoh, the lord of the stakes﴾. It is said: he had four stakes, and when he became angry with a person and wished to punish him, he would stretch his hands and feet on the ground with those stakes.

In the narrative: he subjected his wife Asiya to this same kind of punishment, and placed a rock upon her chest until she died. And it is related from some of them: he had four pillars, to which he would bind a man by his hands and feet.

It is also said: "lord of the stakes" means: lord of firm sovereignty. The poet said:

(In the shade of a king whose stakes are firmly set...)

Al-Sam'ani's commentary on Surah 89, verse 11:

And His saying: ﴿Those who transgressed in the lands﴾, meaning: they exceeded the limit through acts of disobedience. It is also said: they persisted in them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 89, verses 12–13:

And His saying: ﴿So they multiplied corruption therein, and your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾. That is: He punished them. It was also said: He made their punishment take the place of the whip (sawt) among the punishments. And it is reported from some of them that they used to extend the beating with whips until death, the most severe torment. Thus the mention of the punishment here is by the mention of the whip, in the sense that it reached its utmost limit in their punishment.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 89, verses 12–13:

And His saying: ﴿So they multiplied corruption therein, and your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾. That is: He punished them. It was also said: He made their punishment take the place of the whip (sawt) among the punishments. And it is reported from some of them that they used to extend the beating with whips until death, the most severe torment. Thus the mention of the punishment here is by the mention of the whip, in the sense that it reached its utmost limit in their punishment.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 89, verse 14:

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾ means: to Him is the return of creation and their final destination, and the meaning is that no one escapes from Him. It is reported from al-Hasan that He is on the lookout over the deeds of the servants. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that His saying ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾ means: He hears and sees. And from him also: that over Jahannam there are seven bridges (qanatir), so they are questioned at the first bridge about faith, at the second about prayer, at the third about zakat, at the fourth about fasting in Ramadan, at the fifth about the Hajj and 'Umrah, at the sixth about maintaining ties of kinship, and at the seventh about wrongful dealings (mazalim).

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾ is the place where the oath falls.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 89, verse 15:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him and honours him and bestows favours upon him, he says, "My Lord has honoured me."﴾ The verse was revealed concerning Umayya ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi. It is also said: this applies in general.

His words ﴿he says, "My Lord has honoured me"﴾ mean: "I am honoured by Him, since He has given me these favours."

And His saying: ﴿But as for man, when his Lord tests him and restricts his provision for him﴾, that is, He constricted his provision upon him.

[And His saying] ﴿Then he says, "My Lord has humiliated me!"﴾, that is, He did to me what He did because I am contemptible to Him. The meaning is that they supposed that Allah honours with wealth and humiliates with poverty.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 89, verse 17:

And His saying: ﴿Nay!﴾ is a rejection of what they say, meaning: Allah does not honour with wealth, nor humiliate with poverty; rather He honours with obedience and humiliates with disobedience. And on the authority of Ka'b al-Ahbar (tabi'i, a convert from Judaism known as a transmitter of Isra'iliyyat), he said: "Indeed I find in some of the books that Allah, exalted is He, says: Were it not that I grieve My believing servant, I would crown the head of the disbeliever with crowns, so it would never ache, and no vein from it would throb with pain."

And His saying: ﴿But you do not honour the orphan﴾ mentions what the disbelievers do, for which they deserve punishment, in His saying: ﴿You do not honour the orphan.﴾ Regarding it there are two opinions. The first: it is their consuming of the orphans' wealth. The second: it is their failure to show kindness to them.

And His saying: ﴿And do not urge one another to feed the poor﴾, meaning: they do not urge (others). It has also been recited: "wa-la tahāḍḍūna ʿalā ṭaʿām al-miskīn" (and do not urge one another to feed the poor), meaning: they do not urge one another to do so.

And their saying: ﴿And you devour the inheritance, devouring greedily﴾. Al-turath (the inheritance) and al-warith (the heir) have the same meaning, and it is al-mirath (inheritance).

And their saying: ﴿devouring greedily﴾ means: by mixing the lawful with the unlawful.

Mujahid said: ﴿greedily﴾ means: wholesale, gathering part to part and devouring it completely.

And His saying: ﴿And you love wealth with an abundant love﴾, meaning: much. It is recited with both the ta' (second person, "you love") and the ya' (third person, "they love"). Whoever recites it with the ya', it is on the basis of narration (khabar, a report about others); whoever recites it with the ta', it is on the basis of direct address (khitab).
"The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Nay, when the earth is crushed, crushed to powder﴾. That is: broken and pounded to fine dust."

and His saying: ﴿And your Lord comes﴾. This is among the mutashabih (ambiguous verses) in which one believes without interpreting (yufassar). Some of them have interpreted it as: "the command of your Lord comes." The correct view is what we have mentioned.

And His saying: ﴿and the angels in ranks, rank upon rank﴾. That is: in rows (ṣufūf).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 89, verse 23:

And His saying: ﴿And Hell will be brought on that Day﴾. And in some reports from the Prophet (ﷺ) it is related: "Hell will be brought forth bridled with seventy thousand bridles, and the angels will drag it. It will be set up over the whole Throne, and then the prophets will fall to their knees, and each one will say: 'My soul! My soul!'"

This report is gharib (rare, with a weak or single chain), and it is known from someone other than the Messenger.

His saying: ﴿On that Day man will remember, but how will the remembrance benefit him?﴾ That is: he will take heed (yatta'iz). And how can he take heed (al-ittiʿaz)? That is, how will taking heed benefit him?

"And His saying: ﴿He will say, "Oh, I wish I had sent forth for my life"﴾, meaning: for my afterlife. This is in the sense of His saying: ﴿And indeed, the Last Abode is the true life﴾, meaning the enduring life. The meaning here is: for my life in the Hereafter."

And His saying: ﴿So on that Day none will punish as He punishes﴾, with a kasra (on the dhāl), and this is the more well-known of the two readings. Its meaning: no one punishes in this world with the like of what Allah punishes with in the Hereafter, and no one binds in this world with the like of what He binds with in the Hereafter. And it has been read: "fa-yawma'idhin lā yu'adhdhibu 'adhābahu aḥad" with a fatḥa on the dhāl, and its meaning: no one punishes with the like of the punishment of this disbeliever, or no one punishes with the like of the punishment of this category of disbelievers. Likewise His saying: ﴿yawthiqu﴾ with a fatḥa on the thā'.

And His saying: ﴿So on that Day none will punish as He punishes﴾, with a kasra (on the dhāl), and this is the more well-known of the two readings. Its meaning: no one punishes in this world with the like of what Allah punishes with in the Hereafter, and no one binds in this world with the like of what He binds with in the Hereafter. And it has been read: "fa-yawma'idhin lā yu'adhdhibu 'adhābahu aḥad" with a fatḥa on the dhāl, and its meaning: no one punishes with the like of the punishment of this disbeliever, or no one punishes with the like of the punishment of this category of disbelievers. Likewise His saying: ﴿yawthiqu﴾ with a fatḥa on the thā'.

Almighty Allah's saying: ﴿O soul at rest﴾, that is, the believing soul that is settled (calm). It is also said: at rest in regard to the promise of its Lord. It was also said: the intended meaning of "soul" (nafs) here is the spirit (rūḥ). And it is said: it refers to the whole human being when he is a believer.

"And His saying: ﴿Return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing [to Him]﴾ means: she is pleased with Allah, and Allah pleases her with respect to herself."

It is related in some reports that two angels come to the believer at the time of the taking of his soul, and they say: "Come out, O soul, to rest and sweet provision, and a Lord who is not angry."
And His saying: ﴿Enter among My servants﴾ — meaning: along with My servants.

﴿وادخلي جنتي﴾ And this saying will be on the Day of Resurrection.

It is also recited in the irregular reading (al-shadhdh, a reading not transmitted through the accepted channels): "فادخلي فِي عَبدِي" ("enter among My servants"). That is, it is said to the soul (al-nafs, i.e., the spirit): "Enter among My servants," meaning into his body, "and enter My Paradise," and that is at the Resurrection.

From Ikrimah: when this verse was revealed, Abu Bakr said, "Indeed this is a great good." The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Indeed, the angel will say it to you."

From Abu Burayda: the verse was revealed concerning Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib (may Allah be pleased with him).

From some of them: it was revealed concerning Khubayb ibn Adi (may Allah be pleased with him), who was taken captive and crucified in Makkah. He was the first to establish praying two rak'ahs at the time of crucifixion, and he is the one who said:

(I do not care, when I am killed as a Muslim,
on which side I fall for the sake of God.
And that is for the sake of God; and if He wills,
He will bless the torn pieces of my flesh.)

From Amir ibn Qays: he came as a delegation to Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) and sat at his door. Uthman came out to him and saw a Bedouin wearing a bitt (a coarse woollen cloak), but he did not recognise him. So he said, "Where is your Lord, O Bedouin?" He said, "In the place of watching."

Uthman was silenced, and this is in accordance with His saying: ﴿إن ربك لبالمرصاد﴾ ("Indeed your Lord is ever watchful"). And Allah knows best.
